claims.text: Toughness retention at elevated temperatures in high-entropy alloys is governed by grain-boundary morphology.
Inducing serrated grain boundaries can reduce local strain concentration.
Serrated grain boundaries delay intergranular crack initiation.
Serrated grain boundaries maintain elevated-temperature ductility and extend creep rupture life.
The initial SLM high-entropy alloy has straight, nearly planar grain boundaries.
The initial SLM high-entropy alloy undergoes a hot-ductility drop at elevated temperature.
Reducing the cooling rate during solution heat treatment promotes coarsening of precipitates.
Coarsened precipitates interfere with mobile grain boundaries and induce a serrated grain-boundary morphology.
The relevant precipitates are L1₂-structured gamma-prime precipitates.
The controlled structural mediator is a transformation from straight to serrated grain boundaries.
Serrated boundaries distribute local strains more evenly than straight boundaries.
More even strain distribution reduces stress localization and resistance to intergranular cracking is increased.
Weak intergranular sites typically cause brittle failure at high temperatures in the target alloy.
At 650°C, serrated grain boundaries will increase tensile fracture strain by approximately 3.5 times relative to straight boundaries.
At 650°C, serrated grain boundaries will increase creep rupture life by hundreds of times relative to straight boundaries.
The reported reference improvement in creep rupture life is approximately 400-fold.
The hypothesis should apply to SLM-processed high-entropy alloys tested near 650°C when grain-boundary-controlled mechanisms dominate.
Applicability to other processing routes, substantially different temperatures, alloy compositions, or precipitate chemistries is uncertain.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in both tensile ductility and creep rupture life, or failure to observe different strain-localization patterns, would falsify the hypothesis.
